title: Server Side JavaScript
summary: Node.js on the server: one busy thread that never waits, modules that load once, the node and npm commands, core modules and frameworks, and package.json versions you can trust.

lessons.title: Node.js: what it is and how modules load
lessons.objective: Given a scenario and requirements, infer which Node.js implementation is a good solution.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Node.js** runs JavaScript outside the browser, on a server or your laptop. Your code runs on one main thread. Slow jobs, like reading a file or calling a database, are handed to the system. Node serves other work while it waits. That is **non-blocking I/O**.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: One waiter in a busy café. They take an order, pass it to the kitchen, and serve the next table while it cooks. Where it stops: if the waiter has to chop vegetables themselves (heavy math), every table waits.

cards.title: Good fit, bad fit
cards.body: Node shines at **I/O-heavy** work: APIs, chat, streaming, lots of small requests. Long math on the main thread blocks the **event loop**, the loop that runs the next ready job. Move CPU-heavy work to **worker threads** or a **child process**.

cards.title: Not a browser
items: `Buffer` holds raw bytes, like file data

cards.title: CommonJS
cards.body: **CommonJS** is Node's original module system. `require()` loads a file and returns its `module.exports`. `exports.add` adds to that same object.

cards.title: Loaded once
cards.body: Node **caches** a module after the first `require()`. Its top-level code runs once. Every later `require()` of the same file gets the very same object back. Change it in one file, and every file sees the change.

cards.title: ES modules in Node
cards.body: **ES modules** use `import` and `export`. Node loads a file that way when it ends in `.mjs`, or ends in `.js` under `"type": "module"` in package.json. `.cjs` always means CommonJS. ES modules have no `require` or `__dirname`; use `import.meta.url`. Relative imports need the full name: `./math.js`.

`exports = { add }` exports nothing. It only points the local name at a new object. `require()` still returns `module.exports`, which stays empty. To replace the whole export, write `module.exports = { add }`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"One waiter, many tables."** Node never waits, so don't make it cook. For modules: change `module.exports`, never reassign `exports`.

terms.say: A program that runs JavaScript outside a web browser. People use it to build servers and command-line tools.
Asking for slow input or output, like a file, and not standing still while it comes. Node does other work and picks up the answer later.
The loop inside Node that keeps picking the next ready job and running it. If one job takes too long, everything else waits.
Extra helpers inside one Node program. Each runs JavaScript on its own, so heavy math there does not freeze the main thread.
A separate program that Node starts and talks to. Heavy work there runs beside Node instead of blocking it.
The name for the global object that works everywhere. In a browser it is the window; in Node it is the object also called global.
Node's object about the running program. It holds the command-line words, the environment settings, and a way to stop the program.
Node's older way to share code between files. One file sets module.exports, and another file gets it back with require().
The object a CommonJS file hands to whoever calls require() on it. Whatever you put there is what other files get.
The standard JavaScript way to share code between files, using import and export. Browsers and Node both understand it.

lessons.title: Node and npm on the command line
lessons.objective: Given a scenario and requirements, infer which Node.js CLI command is a good solution.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: You run Node and its tools from a terminal. `node` runs JavaScript files and quick snippets. **npm**, the Node package manager, installs packages and runs your project's scripts. **npx** runs a command that comes from a package. If the package isn't installed, it offers to fetch it.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A kitchen. `node` is the stove: it cooks what you hand it. npm is the grocery service and the shopping list. npx borrows a gadget for one recipe. Where it stops: npx keeps a cached copy, so the gadget is not fully gone afterwards.

cards.title: Running code with node
items: `node -e "code"` runs a snippet; it prints only what you log
`node -p "1 + 1"` runs it and prints the result
`node` alone opens the **REPL**, a live prompt
`node -r dotenv/config app.js` loads a module first

cards.title: Debugging
cards.code:
node --inspect app.js      # run; a debugger can attach
node --inspect-brk app.js  # also pause before line 1
node inspect app.js        # built-in terminal debugger
cards.body: `--inspect` lets a debugger such as Chrome DevTools attach (open `chrome://inspect`). `--inspect-brk` also pauses before your code starts, so you can set breakpoints first.

cards.title: Everyday npm
items: `npm init -y` makes package.json with default answers
`npm install -g` installs a tool for the whole machine
`npm ci` installs exactly what the **lock file** says

cards.title: Scripts
cards.code:
npm run build   # runs "build" from "scripts"
npm test        # "test" needs no "run"
npm start       # neither does "start"
npx eslint .    # run a package's command
cards.body: `npm run <name>` runs any script in package.json. Only `test`, `start`, `stop` and `restart` have shortcuts without `run`.
"`npm test` works, so `npm deploy` will too." No. A custom script always needs `npm run deploy`. Another classic: `node -e "1 + 1"` prints nothing. Use `-p` to print the result.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"-e evals, -p prints, -brk brakes."** And: `test` and `start` skip `run`; every other script says `npm run`.

terms.say: The tool that comes with Node for getting packages. It downloads code other people shared and runs the scripts in your project.
A helper that runs a command from a package. If the package is not in your project, it can fetch it first.
A live prompt where you type JavaScript and see the answer right away. It stands for Read, Eval, Print, Loop.
A Node flag that opens a door for a debugger. Then a tool like Chrome DevTools can pause and look inside your program.
Like --inspect, but Node also pauses before your first line runs. That gives you time to set breakpoints.
The command that creates a new package.json file. With -y it uses the default answers and asks you nothing.
A package you need only while building or testing, like a test tool. People who install your package do not get it.
An install command for build servers. It installs exactly what the lock file lists, and stops with an error if the files disagree.
The file package-lock.json. It writes down the exact version of every package installed, so every install can match.
The command that runs a script listed in package.json, by its name. For example, npm run build.

lessons.title: Core modules and popular frameworks
lessons.objective: Know the core Node.js modules and given requirements, infer which Node.js library/framework is a good solution.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Node ships with **core modules**: built-in tools you load without installing anything. You can add the `node:` prefix, like `require('node:fs')`, to show it is built in. For bigger apps, people add a **framework** from npm, such as Express.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A new kitchen comes with a stove, a sink and knives: the core modules. A framework is a meal-kit service that also tells you how to lay out the meal. Where it stops: you can cook without a kit, and many apps use only core modules.

cards.title: Core modules to know
items: `http` and `https`: make a server or send a request
`path`: build file paths safely on any system

cards.title: Three ways to read a file
cards.body: A **sync** call blocks the event loop: nothing else runs until it finishes. Fine in a start-up script, bad in a busy server. Callbacks get the **error first**, then the data.

cards.title: Events
cards.body: An **EventEmitter** calls its listeners **synchronously**, in the order they were added. `once` listens one time. Emitting `'error'` with no listener throws.

cards.title: Streams
cards.body: A **stream** moves data in small chunks instead of all at once. There are four kinds: Readable, Writable, Duplex and Transform. Connect them with `pipe()` or `stream.pipeline()`. `pipeline` also passes on errors and cleans up. Streams keep memory low, even for huge files.

cards.title: Frameworks: pick by need
items: **Fastify**: minimal and fast, with JSON schemas
**Next.js**: a React framework that can render pages on the server

cards.body: Calling `readFileSync` on a huge file inside a request handler. Every other user waits until it finishes, and the whole file sits in memory. Use the async API, or a stream for big files.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Sync stops the shop."** In a server, use callbacks, promises or streams. And `emit` is a phone call, not a letter: listeners run right away.

terms.say: Tools that come built into Node, like fs and http. You can use them without installing anything.
Node's built-in file system module. It reads, writes and deletes files and folders.
A built-in module that joins and splits file paths correctly, on Windows and on Linux alike.
A Node object that shouts named events. Other code listens for a name, and its function runs when that event is shouted.
A helper from util. It wraps an old callback-style function so it returns a promise instead, and you can await it.
Right now, in order, before the next line runs. Nothing else happens until it is done.
A way to move data in small pieces, like water through a pipe, instead of carrying it all at once in one bucket.
A helper that connects streams in a row. If one breaks, it tells you and closes the others.
A popular, small Node framework for web servers and APIs. You add routes and middleware to handle requests.
Small functions that a request passes through, one after another, before the answer goes back. Each can check, change or stop it.

lessons.title: npm packages: package.json, versions and the lock file
lessons.objective: Given a scenario and requirements, distinguish which Node.Js Package Management solution is the most fitting.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Every Node project has a **package.json**: its ID card and shopping list. It names the project, lists the packages it needs and holds its scripts. npm reads it and installs those packages into `node_modules`. Another file, **package-lock.json**, records the exact versions that were installed.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: package.json is a recipe: "eggs, any brand from this year". The lock file is last week's receipt: these exact eggs. Shop from the receipt and every kitchen cooks the same meal. Where it stops: npm rewrites the receipt for you when you add a package.

cards.title: Three kinds of dependencies
items: **devDependencies**: needed only to build or test (`jest`, `eslint`)
**peerDependencies**: a plugin names the host package it works with
When others install your package, they do not get your devDependencies

cards.title: A package.json
cards.body: `"private": true` blocks publishing by mistake. `main` is the entry file. `pretest` runs by itself before `test`. `name` and `version` are required only to publish.

cards.title: Version ranges
items: **Semver**: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; a new major may break you

cards.title: The lock file
cards.body: **package-lock.json** pins the exact version of every package, even the packages your packages use. **Commit it.** `npm ci` installs exactly from it. It deletes `node_modules` first, never changes either file, and fails if the two files disagree. That makes it right for build servers.

cards.title: Staying safe
cards.body: `npm audit` checks your packages against a list of known security problems. `npm audit fix` moves them to safe versions where your ranges allow. `npm outdated` shows which packages have newer versions.
"`^1.2.3` means exactly 1.2.3." No: the **caret** allows any newer 1.x.x. Another trap: putting Jest in `dependencies`. Test tools belong in `devDependencies`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Caret keeps the major. Tilde keeps the minor."** The ^ hat lets minor and patch move; the ~ wave lets only the patch drift. And build servers use `npm ci`.

terms.say: A project's ID card. It lists the name, the packages the project needs, and its scripts.
A file npm writes that lists the exact version of every installed package. Share it so everyone installs the very same ones.
The folder where npm puts the packages it downloads. You never edit it by hand, and you do not commit it.
The packages your app needs while it runs. Anyone who installs your app gets them too.
Packages you need only while building or testing, like Jest. They are not installed for people who use your package.
A note from a plugin saying: I work with this host package, and I will use your copy of it.
Short for semantic versioning. A version has three numbers: major, minor and patch. A new major can break things.
The ^ sign before a version. It allows newer minor and patch versions, but never a new major one.
A strict install for build servers. It wipes node_modules and installs exactly what the lock file says.
A command that checks your packages against a list of known security holes and reports what it finds.

flashcards.front: What kind of work is Node.js good at, and what kind is it bad at?
flashcards.back: Good: I/O-heavy work like APIs, chat and many small requests. Bad: long CPU-heavy math on the main thread. Move that to worker threads or a child process.
It only points the local `exports` name at a new object. `require()` returns `module.exports`, which stays empty. Use `module.exports = { add }` instead.

flashcards.front: What happens when two files `require()` the same module?
flashcards.back: The module runs once and is cached. Both files get the very same object, so a change made by one is seen by the other.

flashcards.front: How does Node know a file is an ES module?
flashcards.back: It ends in `.mjs`, or ends in `.js` with `"type": "module"` in the nearest package.json. `.cjs` always means CommonJS.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `node -e` and `node -p`?
flashcards.back: `node -e` runs code and prints only what you log. `node -p` runs code and prints the result for you.

flashcards.front: When do you use `--inspect-brk` instead of `--inspect`?
flashcards.back: When the bug happens right at the start. `--inspect-brk` pauses before your first line, so you can set breakpoints first.

flashcards.front: Which npm scripts can you run without `run`?
flashcards.back: `test`, `start`, `stop` and `restart`. Every other script needs `npm run <name>`, like `npm run build`.
It runs a command from a package. It uses the copy in your project if there is one. If not, it asks, then fetches the package.

flashcards.front: Why are sync calls like `readFileSync` risky in a server?
flashcards.back: They block the event loop. No other request is served until the call finishes. Use callbacks, promises or streams instead.

flashcards.front: When does an `EventEmitter` run its listeners?
flashcards.back: Right away, inside `emit()`, one after another in the order they were added. Emitting `'error'` with no listener throws.

flashcards.front: Why use a stream for a big file?
flashcards.back: A stream moves the file in small chunks, so memory stays low. `stream.pipeline()` connects streams and handles errors and cleanup.
Express or Koa: minimal, with middleware. Fastify: minimal and fast. NestJS: structured and TypeScript-first. Next.js: a React framework that can render pages on the server.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `dependencies` and `devDependencies`?
flashcards.back: `dependencies` are needed while the app runs. `devDependencies` are only for building and testing, like Jest, and are not installed for people who use your package.
`^1.4.2`: 1.4.2 up to, but not including, 2.0.0. `~1.4.2`: 1.4.2 up to, but not including, 1.5.0.
It pins the exact version of every package. With it, `npm ci` gives every machine the same install.

flashcards.front: What does `npm ci` do differently from `npm install`?
flashcards.back: It needs a lock file, deletes `node_modules` first, installs exactly what the lock says, never changes either file, and fails if they disagree.

questions.q: How does Node.js handle many requests at the same time?
options: It starts a new operating system thread for each incoming request
It runs JavaScript on one thread and hands slow I/O to the system
It finishes each request fully before it reads the next one
It runs each request inside its own copy of the V8 engine
questions.explain: Node runs your JavaScript on one main thread. Slow I/O, like files and networks, is handed off, and the event loop picks up the results later.
wrong: Node does not make a thread per request; one thread serves them all.
Node starts other requests while one waits on I/O.
All requests share one engine and one main thread.
questions.source: Node.js docs: The Node.js Event Loop

questions.q: Which of these is a global you can use in Node.js but not in a browser page?
questions.explain: Node has no page, so it has no DOM objects. It gives you `process` instead, with `argv`, `env` and `exit()`.
wrong: `document` is the browser page; Node has no DOM.
`window` exists only in browsers; Node uses `globalThis`.
`alert` is a browser pop-up; Node has no page to show it on.

questions.q: Both files are in the same folder. What does `node app.js` log?
questions.explain: A module is cached after its first `require()`, so its code runs once. `a` and `b` are the same function sharing one `count`, so the third call returns 3.
wrong: That would need a fresh `count` for `b`, but the module is cached.
Two calls happened before `b()`, so it adds one more.
`count` is in scope for the function the module exports.

questions.q: What does `node app.js` log?
questions.explain: Assigning to `exports` only rebinds a local name. `require()` returns `module.exports`, which is still an empty object, so `greet.hello` is `undefined`.
wrong: The function was never put on `module.exports`.
`typeof` an arrow function would be `'function'`, but here nothing was exported.
Reading a missing property gives `undefined`; it does not throw.

questions.q: A Node.js API also resizes large photos on each upload. Under load, all other requests stall while a photo is processed. What is the best fix?
options: Wrap the resize code in an `async` function
Run the resize code in a `Worker` from `worker_threads`
questions.explain: Heavy CPU work blocks the one main thread, however you schedule it. A worker thread runs it in parallel, so the event loop stays free.
wrong: An `async` function still runs its sync math on the main thread.
The delay only moves the blocking to a moment later.
A promise callback still runs on the main thread and blocks it.

questions.q: The file `paths.mjs` holds this one line. What happens when it runs with Node.js?
options: It prints the folder that holds the file
questions.explain: A `.mjs` file is an ES module, and ES modules have no `__dirname`. Reading an undeclared name throws a `ReferenceError`; build the path from `import.meta.url` instead.
wrong: That is what a CommonJS file would print.
The name is not declared at all, so it throws instead.
No such variable exists in ES modules, so nothing is printed.

questions.q: A developer on Node.js 16 wants to use `import` and `export` in a project file. Which two approaches make Node.js load the file as an ES module? (Choose 2)
options: Put `'use strict'` at the top of the file
Set `"main"` to the file in package.json
questions.explain: Node picks the module system from the file extension and the nearest package.json. `.mjs`, or `.js` under `"type": "module"`, means ES module.
wrong: `.cjs` forces CommonJS, the opposite.
Strict mode does not change the module system.
`main` only names the entry file; it does not set the module type.

questions.q: In a Node.js ES module, which line loads the local file `utils.js` from the same folder?
questions.explain: ES modules in Node need the full file name in relative imports. Leaving off `.js` gives a "module not found" error.
wrong: Node does not guess the extension for ES module imports.
A bare name looks in `node_modules`, not in this folder.
This mixes two syntaxes and is not valid JavaScript.

questions.q: A Node.js service gets thousands of small requests a second. Each one reads a row from a database and returns it as JSON. A teammate wants to start a new thread per request "so the database calls don't block". What should the lead say?
options: Good idea: Node serves one request until its database call returns
Better: switch the database driver to sync calls so each one finishes fast
Better: use `cluster` to start one new process for every request
Not needed: Node waits on the database without blocking its one thread
questions.explain: Database calls are I/O, and Node waits on I/O without blocking. One thread can serve thousands of requests that mostly wait, which is exactly what Node is good at.
wrong: Node serves other requests while each database call is in flight.
Sync calls would block the event loop and make it far worse.
`cluster` runs a few workers, about one per CPU core, not one per request.
questions.source: Node.js docs: The Node.js Event Loop

questions.q: All three files are in one folder. What does `node main.js` log?
questions.explain: Modules are cached, so every `require('./config')` returns the same object. `a.js` changed it first, so `main.js` sees `'debug'`.
wrong: The module does not reload; it returns the object `a.js` already changed.
The object is exported, so `level` is there.
Each file has its own scope, so the two `cfg` names never clash.

questions.q: Which two statements about CommonJS modules in Node.js are true? (Choose 2)
options: `exports = { x: 1 }` replaces the object that `require()` returns
`exports.x = 1` adds `x` to the object that `require()` returns
A module's top-level code runs again on every `require()` call
`require()` loads the file synchronously and returns `module.exports`
`require()` returns a promise that resolves to the module
questions.explain: `exports` starts as a shortcut to `module.exports`, so adding properties works. `require()` is synchronous and returns `module.exports`, cached after the first load.
wrong: Reassigning `exports` only rebinds the local name.
The module is cached, so its code runs once.
That describes dynamic `import()`, not `require()`.

questions.q: What does `node app.js` log?
questions.explain: Assigning `module.exports` breaks its link to `exports`. The later `exports.name` goes onto the old object, which nobody returns, so `s.name` is `undefined`.
wrong: `name` was added to the old object, not the exported one.
`area` is on the exported object, so it returns 3.
Both reads are safe; a missing property is just `undefined`.

questions.q: A developer copies this CommonJS file into a project whose package.json has `"type": "module"`. It now fails on its first line. Which change makes it work as an ES module?
questions.code:
const path = require('node:path');
const dataDir = path.join(__dirname, 'data');
options: Use `import path from 'node:path'` and keep `__dirname` as it is
Use `import path from 'node:path'` and build the folder from `import.meta.url`
Keep `require()` and add `'use strict'` as the first line
Keep both lines and rename the file to end in `.mjs`
questions.explain: ES modules have neither `require` nor `__dirname`. Import the module, and get the folder from `import.meta.url`, for example with `fileURLToPath`.
wrong: `__dirname` does not exist in ES modules either.
Strict mode does not bring `require` back.
`.mjs` is also an ES module, so both lines still fail.

questions.q: Which command prints `1024` without any `console.log` in the code?
questions.explain: `-p` (print) runs the code and prints the result. `-e` (eval) runs it but prints only what the code logs.
wrong: `-e` runs it silently; nothing is logged.
`-r` preloads a module by name, so this fails.
`--inspect` turns on the debugger and expects a file.

questions.q: A developer wants a new package.json with every default answer, without being asked any questions. Which command does that?
questions.explain: `npm init` creates package.json. The `-y` (yes) flag accepts every default.
wrong: `npm install` installs packages; it does not create package.json from defaults.
`npm start` runs the start script.
`npm ci` needs an existing lock file and creates nothing.

questions.q: A bug shows up in the first lines of a Node.js script, before a developer can set any breakpoint in Chrome DevTools. Which command should they start the script with?
questions.explain: `--inspect-brk` opens the debugger and pauses before the first line of your code. You get time to set breakpoints.
wrong: `--inspect` starts running at once, so the first lines finish before you attach.
`-e` treats `app.js` as code to run, not a file.
`--check` only checks the syntax; it never runs or debugs the code.

questions.q: A package.json has these scripts. Which two commands run one of them? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: `npm run <name>` runs any script. `start` also has a shortcut, so `npm start` works without `run`.
wrong: There is no `npm lint` command; custom scripts need `run`.
`node` looks for a file named `lint`; it does not read scripts.
`npx` would look for a package called `run`.

questions.q: A build server must install exactly the versions in `package-lock.json`, and stop with an error if it does not match `package.json`. Which command fits?
questions.explain: `npm ci` installs exactly from the lock file. If the lock and package.json disagree, it fails instead of fixing the lock.
wrong: `npm install` may update the lock file to fit package.json.
`npm update` moves packages to newer versions.
`--save-exact` only changes how new ranges are written.

questions.q: A developer runs `node greet.js Ana`. What does it log?
questions.explain: `process.argv` starts with the path to `node` and the path to the script. Your own words start at index 2.
wrong: The array also holds the node path and the script path.
There are three items: node, the script, and `Ana`.
Index 2 holds the first word you typed, `Ana`.

questions.q: ESLint is installed in a project's `devDependencies`. There is no script for it. Which command runs the project's ESLint?
questions.explain: `npx` runs a command from a package. It uses the copy in the project's `node_modules` first.
wrong: `node` looks for a file named `eslint`.
`eslint` is not an npm command.
`npm run` needs a script called `eslint`, and there is none.

questions.q: Which two commands add `jest` to `devDependencies`? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: `--save-dev`, or its short form `-D`, saves the package under `devDependencies`.
wrong: `-g` installs a global tool and does not touch package.json.
With no flag, npm saves it to `dependencies`.
`npm ci` installs a whole project and takes no package name.

questions.q: A developer types `node` with no file name and presses Enter. What happens?
options: Node runs `index.js` in the current folder
Node prints its help text and exits
An interactive prompt, the REPL, opens
Node runs the `start` script from package.json
questions.explain: With no file, `node` opens the REPL. You type JavaScript and see each result right away.
wrong: Node never picks a file by itself.
Help needs `node --help`.
Scripts run through npm, not `node`.

questions.q: Which two commands print `2` in the terminal? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: `-p` prints the result of the code. `-e` prints only what the code itself logs.
wrong: `-e` runs the sum but prints nothing.
`-c` checks the syntax of a file; it treats the text as a file name.
`-r` tries to preload a module named `1 + 1` and fails.

questions.q: A developer starts an app on a remote test server with the command below. From their own laptop, Chrome DevTools cannot connect to it. What is the most likely reason?
questions.code:
node --inspect app.js
# Debugger listening on ws://127.0.0.1:9229/...
options: Chrome DevTools can debug browser tabs, never Node
The inspector listens on `127.0.0.1`, so only that machine can reach it
`--inspect` needs `node inspect` running on the laptop as well
questions.explain: By default the inspector listens on `127.0.0.1:9229`, the server's own local address. Reach it safely through an SSH tunnel; opening it to the network is risky.
wrong: `--inspect` works alone; `-brk` only adds a pause at the start.
DevTools attaches to Node through `chrome://inspect`.
`node inspect` is a separate terminal debugger, not a client for DevTools.

questions.q: A developer wants `.env` values loaded before `app.js` runs, without editing `app.js`. The `dotenv` package is installed. Which command does this?
questions.explain: `-r` (`--require`) preloads a module before the main script. `dotenv/config` reads `.env` into `process.env` as it loads.
wrong: Flags after the file name go to the script in `process.argv`, not to Node.
`-e` runs its text as code, so `dotenv/config` throws a `ReferenceError`.
`--inspect` sets a debugger host, not a module to load.

questions.q: Jest 28 is in a project's `devDependencies`, and `npm install` has run. Nothing is installed globally. In the project folder, typing `jest` gives "command not found". Why, and what runs the project's Jest without adding a script?
options: npm skipped Jest because it is a devDependency; run `npm install` again
Dev tools cannot run as commands; move Jest to `dependencies`
`jest` must go through npm here; type `npm jest` instead
The shell does not look in `node_modules/.bin`; use `npx jest`
questions.explain: npm puts each package's commands in `node_modules/.bin`, and the shell does not search that folder. `npx` looks there first, so `npx jest` runs the project's Jest 28.
wrong: A plain `npm install` already installs `devDependencies`.
Both kinds put their commands in the same `node_modules/.bin` folder.
`jest` is not an npm command, so npm stops with an error.

questions.q: Which core module builds file paths that work on both Windows and Linux?
questions.explain: `path` joins and resolves paths with the right separator for the system.
wrong: `fs` reads and writes files; it does not build paths.
`os` reports facts about the machine.
`util` holds general helpers like `promisify`.

questions.q: Which core module gives you the `EventEmitter` class?
questions.explain: `EventEmitter` comes from `events`. Many other core objects, like streams and servers, are built on it.
wrong: Streams use `EventEmitter`, but the class lives in `events`.
`util` holds helpers like `promisify`.
`http` servers emit events, but the class is not defined there.

questions.q: On Linux, what does this code log?
questions.explain: `path.join` glues the parts with `/` and then tidies the result. `..` steps back out of `app`, leaving `/srv/logs/today.txt`.
wrong: `join` tidies the path, so `..` is resolved.
`..` goes up one folder only, out of `app`.
The leading `/` stays, and `..` removes `app`.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: `emit()` calls its listeners synchronously, right away. So `A` logs between `B` and `C`.
wrong: The listener runs only when `emit()` is called, after `B`.
`emit()` is not queued for later; it runs before `C`.
Nothing logs `A` before `B` runs.

questions.q: Many users download a 1 GB video at once. With this code, the server runs out of memory. What is the best fix?
options: Use `fs.readFileSync` so the read finishes first
Raise the http server's timeout to give it time
Read it with `fs/promises` and `await` the result
questions.explain: A stream sends the file in small chunks, so the whole file never sits in memory. `pipe` also slows down when the client is slow.
wrong: It still loads the whole file, and it also blocks the event loop.
Time is not the problem; memory is.
The promise API still loads the whole file into memory.

questions.q: An old library has `getUser(id, (err, user) => {})`. A developer wants to use `await` with it. Which core helper turns it into a function that returns a promise?
questions.explain: `util.promisify` wraps a function whose callback gets the error first. The new function returns a promise you can `await`.
wrong: That makes a promise holding the function itself, not its result.
`events.once` waits for an event from an emitter, not a callback.
`new Promise` would call `getUser` with `resolve` and `reject` as `id` and the callback.

questions.q: A startup needs a small REST API. They want a framework that imposes little structure and adds features through middleware. Which two fit best? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: Express and Koa are minimal server frameworks. You build them up with middleware, one small function per step.
wrong: NestJS gives a strict structure with modules and dependency injection.
Next.js is a React framework for full web apps, not a small API core.
Angular is a front-end framework that runs in the browser.

questions.q: A large team wants a structured, TypeScript-first Node.js server with modules and dependency injection. Which framework fits best?
questions.explain: NestJS is built with TypeScript and organizes an app into modules, controllers and services with dependency injection.
wrong: Express is minimal and leaves the structure to you.
Koa is a small middleware core with no set structure.
Socket.IO adds real-time messages; it is not an app framework.

questions.q: A Node.js step must read text in and write it out in upper case, so it can sit between two others in a pipe. Which stream type is made for this?
questions.explain: A Transform stream is both readable and writable, and its output is computed from its input. That is exactly a filter in a pipe.
wrong: A Readable stream only produces data.
A Writable stream only takes data in.
An emitter sends events but has no stream methods like `pipe`.

questions.q: A Node.js script must run the system command `git rev-parse HEAD` and read what it prints. Which core module does that?
questions.explain: `child_process` starts other programs, for example with `exec` or `spawn`, and gives you their output.
wrong: `os` reports machine facts like CPUs and memory.
Worker threads run JavaScript, not system commands.
`process` describes the current program; it does not start others.

questions.q: What happens when this script runs?
options: It logs `after`, and the error is ignored
The error is thrown, and `after` never logs
It logs `after`, then reports the error
questions.explain: An `'error'` event with no `'error'` listener is thrown. Here nothing catches it, so the script stops before `after`.
wrong: Node never ignores an `'error'` event without a listener.
The `'done'` listener only runs for `'done'` events.
`emit` is synchronous, so the throw happens at once.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: The `once` listener runs on the first `tick` only. The `on` listener runs both times: 1 + 10 + 10 = 21.
wrong: The `on` listener also runs on the second `tick`.
The `once` listener did run once, adding 1.
`once` removes itself after the first call.

questions.q: Every request to this server reads a large report from disk. Under load, the whole server freezes. Which two changes keep it responsive? (Choose 2)
options: Wrap the handler body in a `try...catch` block
Use `fs.readFile` and call `res.end(data)` in its callback
Make the handler an `async` function and keep the rest
Call `res.end()` first, then read the file
questions.explain: `readFileSync` blocks the event loop for every request. A stream or the callback API reads without blocking, so other requests keep flowing.
wrong: Catching errors does not stop the blocking.
The sync read inside still blocks, even in an `async` function.
The response would end before any data is sent.

questions.q: A developer zips uploads with `src.pipe(gzip).pipe(dest)`. When `src` fails halfway, the error goes unhandled and `dest` stays open. Which change fixes both problems?
options: Add `dest.on('error', handler)` and keep the `pipe` chain
questions.explain: `pipe()` does not pass errors along or close the other streams. `stream.pipeline()` passes on any error to its callback and destroys every stream in the chain.
wrong: The error comes from `src`, and `pipe` still leaves `dest` open.
Sync calls block the event loop and load the whole file.
A bigger buffer changes speed, not error handling.

questions.q: The file `missing.txt` does not exist. What does this code log?
options: An uncaught error stops it before anything logs
questions.explain: `readFile` is async, so `reading` logs first. Its callback gets the error first; a missing file has code `ENOENT`.
wrong: The callback runs only after the read finishes, later.
The error is passed in `err`, so the code is logged.
The callback API passes errors in; it does not throw them.

questions.q: Where should a test tool like Jest go in package.json?
questions.explain: Tools used only to build or test belong in `devDependencies`. The running app does not need them.
wrong: `dependencies` are for code the app needs while it runs.
`peerDependencies` are for plugins naming a host package.
`scripts` holds commands, like `"test": "jest"`, not packages.

questions.q: Which file records the exact version of every installed package, including the packages your packages use?
questions.explain: `package-lock.json` pins the exact version of every package in the tree. package.json holds only ranges for direct dependencies.
wrong: package.json holds ranges, and only for your direct dependencies.
That folder holds runnable commands from packages.
`.npmrc` holds npm settings, like the registry.

questions.q: Which command lists known security vulnerabilities in a project's packages?
questions.explain: `npm audit` checks your packages against a database of known security problems.
wrong: `npm outdated` lists newer versions, not security problems.
`npm doctor` checks that npm itself is set up well.
`npm ls` prints the installed package tree.

questions.q: package.json has this line, and there is no lock file. Which version can a fresh `npm install` choose?
questions.explain: The caret allows newer minor and patch versions, but not a new major. So `^4.17.1` means 4.17.1 or newer, below 5.0.0.
wrong: A lower major is never allowed.
4.17.0 is below the minimum, 4.17.1.
5.0.0 is a new major, which the caret blocks.

questions.q: package.json lists this range. Which two versions satisfy it? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: The tilde allows only patch updates. `~2.4.1` means 2.4.1 or newer, below 2.5.0.
wrong: 2.4.0 is below the minimum, 2.4.1.
A new minor version is outside a tilde range.
A new major is outside a tilde range.

questions.q: A team keeps an internal app in a repository next to their published packages. They want npm to refuse if someone runs `npm publish` on the app by mistake. What should they add to its package.json?
questions.explain: With `"private": true`, npm refuses to publish the package.
wrong: A license only states usage rights; publishing still works.
Any valid version can still be published.
An empty entry file does not block publishing.

questions.q: A developer publishes a plugin for ESLint. The plugin must use the ESLint the host project already has, not bring its own copy. Where should `eslint` go in the plugin's package.json?
questions.explain: `peerDependencies` says which host package, and which versions, the plugin works with. The host project provides it.
wrong: That would give the plugin its own copy of ESLint.
Optional ones are skipped if they fail; the plugin still gets its own copy.
Bundled ones ship inside the plugin, its own copy again.

questions.q: A package.json has these scripts. A developer runs `npm test`. What runs, in order?
options: lint and `jest` at the same time, then `echo done`
questions.explain: npm runs `pre<name>` before a script and `post<name>` after it. So `pretest`, `test` and `posttest` run in that order.
wrong: `pretest` and `posttest` run by themselves around `test`.
`pre` scripts run before, not after.
The scripts run one after another, not at once.

questions.q: A private app's package.json has no `name` and no `version`. What happens when a developer runs `npm install`?
options: npm stops and asks for a name
npm fails until both fields are added
npm installs only if `version` is added
questions.explain: `name` and `version` are required only to publish. A package that is never published can leave them out.
wrong: npm does not ask; that is `npm init`.
The fields are optional unless you publish.
`version` is optional too unless you publish.

questions.q: package.json lists this range. The registry has 0.3.2, 0.3.9 and 0.4.0. On a fresh install with no lock file, which version does npm pick?
questions.explain: Below 1.0.0, the caret keeps the minor number too: `^0.3.2` means below 0.4.0. npm picks the newest match, 0.3.9.
wrong: npm picks the newest version that matches, not the lowest.
With a leading 0, a minor bump counts as breaking, so the caret blocks it.
Ranges work fine for 0.x versions.

questions.q: Builds pass on a developer laptop but fail on the build server, which gets a different version of a nested package. The team commits package.json, but `package-lock.json` is in `.gitignore`. Which two changes make builds repeatable? (Choose 2)
options: Change every range in package.json to `*`
Run `npm ci` on the build server
questions.explain: The lock file pins every package, nested ones too, so it must be committed. `npm ci` then installs exactly from it.
wrong: Updating pulls newer versions, the opposite of repeatable.
`*` accepts any version, so builds would vary more.
The build server would still resolve its own versions.

questions.q: The server code uses `express` and `dayjs`; only the tests use `jest`. Production installs skip `devDependencies`, and the server crashes with "Cannot find module 'dayjs'". What is the fix?
options: Run `npm audit fix` on the server
questions.explain: Code the app needs while it runs belongs in `dependencies`. `dayjs` was in `devDependencies`, so production skipped it.
wrong: Jest is only for tests, so it stays in `devDependencies`.
Then production would skip `express` too.
`npm audit fix` fixes security problems, not missing packages.

questions.q: Which two statements about `npm ci` are true? (Choose 2)
options: It updates package-lock.json to match package.json
It can add one new package, like `npm ci lodash`
It works the same with no lock file at all
It fails when package-lock.json and package.json disagree
questions.explain: `npm ci` starts clean by removing `node_modules`. It never writes to package.json or the lock file, so a mismatch is an error.
wrong: `npm ci` never writes to the lock file.
It installs whole projects only; use `npm install` to add a package.
It needs an existing lock file.
